prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level, a new regime of measurement that now tests gravity and fundamental constants

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part optical lattice clock prize to Katori and Ye, and I hold it with more confidence than in round 1 because the exchange sharpened the argument instead of weakening it. The statutes ask for a discovery or an invention that is experimentally verified, and the lattice clock is an invention with two separable, identifiable steps: Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, which removes the light shift by design for many atoms at once, and Ye's demonstration that this scheme can be driven to about 1e-18 with controlled systematics. The verification is of the strongest kind, because independent clocks in different laboratories are compared against each other and agree, and the results are used for millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on varying constants and dark-matter searches. I take the chair's first question as the real test of the citation: it must say that this is a distinct neutral-atom achievement that has produced measurements nobody could make before, so that it is not read as a third step in the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control chain. Those prizes honoured the comb and single-ion control. Neither honoured trapping an ensemble in a lattice with the perturbation cancelled by design. I also note that six of eight members prefer this configuration with the same two names, which I treat as a signal that the case survives scrutiny from very different fields, and not as a count that substitutes for the science.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is category: a clock is an instrument, and part of the impact, the redefinition of the second, is still prospective. I do not think this is disqualifying, because an invention that opens a door is exactly what the statutes name, and the performance and the intercomparisons do not depend on the redefinition. My reservation I cannot remove is credit. Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and the ion-clock groups are raised by several of us, and every one of us, me included, says we rely on recollection. I have no first-publication record in front of me. If the expert report on the early lattice-clock papers shows that the decisive magic-wavelength proposal or the first demonstration is not covered by Katori and Ye, my position on the names must change, and I would want that checked before the final ballot, not assumed. A second, smaller concern is that the prize would honour a field whose most visible consequence is still a promise, and a committee that wanted to wait for the redefinition could defend that.

responses.point: Kroll holds that the Katori and Ye attribution is solid because the magic-wavelength concept and the record-accuracy realisation are separable steps, that ion-clock work was largely covered in 2012, and that the lattice clocks have had two decades of independent comparison. He also asks whether a prize before the redefinition of the second is timely.
responses.response: I agree with the separability argument, and it is the reason I am willing to write the citation around the invention and its realisation instead of the clock community at large. I would be more careful than you on one point. That the ion-clock community was covered by 2012 is a judgement about the Wineland prize, and it does not settle whether Lemonde or the early strontium groups should be named, which is a question about the first lattice-clock papers. On timing, I do not think the redefinition is a maturity question, because the maturity evidence is the intercomparison of independent clocks, which already exists. I see the redefinition as a consequence the community has chosen to build on. I would not delay the prize for it, and I would not describe the prize in a way that depends on it.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first and ranked the lattice clock fifth, because he sees a risk that a committee which twice rewarded the precision-spectroscopy chain would regard this as a third step. He argues that B001 opens a field without an earlier prize and that independent replication answers the stability question.
responses.response: I take the overlap worry seriously, since I raised it against my own choice, and I think it is answered by what each earlier prize actually honoured. The comb gave a way to count optical cycles, and the ion work gave control of individual quantum systems. Neither gave a method to hold thousands of neutral atoms with the clock transition left unperturbed. That is why I think the citation can be written without overlap. Where I part with you is on maturity. The existence of the correlated phases is well replicated, but the pairing mechanism is open and twist-angle disorder still limits what can be compared between devices, so I would not say the clocks and the moire case are equally settled. I accept that no earlier prize covers moire matter, and I still think B001 is a strong prize for a later year. I agree with you that Bistritzer should stay in the B001 configuration if it is ever chosen.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the clocks first, argues that the 'discovery' is the demonstrated cancellation of systematic shifts for thousands of atoms and what it opens, and says the committee must ask whether this is a discovery or an engineering triumph. He also asks how the citation should be worded.
responses.response: I agree that the wording is the point on which this rests. I would not frame the invention as a clock that is more accurate, because that invites the engineering reading. I would frame it as a new regime of measurement that has already tested gravity at millimetre scales and constrained constants. That is why my citation carries a clause about testing gravity and fundamental constants, and I would like us to keep that clause in any common text. I also want to correct my own round-1 response to you. You asked for the historical record to be checked, and I agreed, but the chair is right that agreeing is not the same as doing it: a statement that two names are clean cannot stand on recollection from all six of us who hold it. I would ask that the expert report address the first magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium demonstrations specifically, so that the committee can say which questions the record settles and which are judgement.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers twisted bilayer graphene because a simple analytical continuum model made a general prediction that experiment tested directly, but names the optical lattice clock as the more mature and less contested choice if the committee finds the discovery not yet settled. He answered my round-1 position by saying that a corrector is a tool and the 1986 electron-microscope prize already covered the instrument, so B030 would need an explicit argument for ranking a tool above a new phase of matter.
responses.response: I accept your challenge on B030 and I withdraw it from my preferred configuration for reasons beyond my recusal. The corrector is a real invention, but the committee would have to argue that it ranks above a discovery in a different category, and only I support it, so I cannot make that argument honestly. I also accept your own conditional: it is in effect what I am saying, that if the committee finds the moire discovery not yet settled, the clock is the more mature choice. Where I still differ from you is that I do not think the open pairing mechanism is a trivial feature of a young field. The prize guards against crediting the wrong people, and for moire matter the earlier flat-band theory and the first experimental authors are difficult within three names. That uncertainty does not exist for the clock to the same degree, which is why I put it ahead.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube to the lattice clock and judges it on the criteria of a new measurement capability, controlled systematics and independent confirmation, and states that he takes B030 seriously but that I am the only member to rank it and the corrector pioneers outside the supplied names make a three-person split harder.
responses.response: I agree with your reasoning on B030, in particular that Krivanek and others outside the supplied names make the credit harder than I suggested in my opening ballot, and I do not push it. On IceCube, which was your own first choice, I thank you for being candid about the unresolved split among Halzen, Karle and Spiering. I still hold what I said in round 1: I cannot be absolutely sure that those three names are the people who did the original work in a collaboration of this size, and I could change only if an expert report documents who led the decisive 2013 analysis steps. I keep it as an alternative, not as my preference, because the source associations are still recent.

uncertainties: Priority among Katori, Ye, Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom for the first magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice-clock demonstrations is still from recollection, and an expert check could change the names.
Whether the committee will accept a clause on gravity and fundamental-constant tests as sufficient to separate the prize from the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
Whether the timing is right before the redefinition of the second, which I treat as a question of timing and not of maturity.
For B001, whether the open pairing mechanism, device variation and earlier flat-band theory justify waiting, which is a matter of judgement that the record will not settle.
For B039, whether credit among Halzen, Karle and Spiering can be documented, which I cannot judge from what I have.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. B030 (aberration-corrected electron optics) is in my own field of electron microscopy and I ranked it first at opening; I would recuse on it and I no longer propose it. For B007 I have held a University of Tokyo fellowship since 2025 and have long exchanges with the Tokyo microscopy community, where Katori works, but I have no personal or research connection to Katori or Ye that I know of, and I see no need to recuse; I flag it for the chair. Goran Johansson is a Chalmers physics colleague, an institutional link that involves no candidate. I report no other conflict.
